title: Training and Attention Efficiency
oneLiner: Big models are limited by memory more than by speed: optimizer bookkeeping, saved intermediate values and the giant word-by-word comparison table of attention all need clever tricks to fit.

what.html:
While a model trains, the GPU has to hold the weights, a gradient for every weight, the optimizer's extra notes, and values saved from the forward pass. Attention adds a table comparing every word with every other word, which grows with the square of the text length. This session covers the tricks that make all of that fit: mixed precision, FlashAttention, Ring Attention and cheaper attention variants.

Everyday versionPacking for a long trip: you can't bring a bigger suitcase, so you roll clothes tightly (16-bit numbers), pack one cube at a time (tiles), and share the load among fellow travellers (several GPUs).

why.html:
• "Will it fit on the GPU?" is the first question in any training plan.
  • These tricks are why 100,000-word contexts are possible at all.
  • The same ideas return when serving models (next two sessions).

how.title: Count what fills memory
how.html: Weights, gradients, optimizer notes, and saved activations. Activations grow with batch size and text length: 2,048 tokens × 8 examples on a 32-layer model is about 73 GB on its own.

how.title: Adam's bill: 16 bytes each
how.html: Weight 4 bytes + gradient 4 + Adam's two notes 8 = 16 bytes per parameter. A 1-billion-parameter model needs about 16 GB before any activations.

how.title: Use 16-bit numbers carefully
how.html: Do the maths in 16-bit (faster, smaller activations) but keep a 32-bit master copy of the weights. Multiply the loss by a big number first so tiny gradients don't round to zero.

how.title: Attention grows as n²
how.html: Every word looks at every other word. Twice the text means four times the work: 2,000 words cost 4× as much as 1,000.

how.title: FlashAttention: work in tiles
how.html: Compute attention one small block at a time in the GPU's fast memory, keeping a running total, so the huge table is never written out. Exactly the same answer, much faster.

how.title: Ring Attention: share the text
how.html: Split a very long text across several GPUs and pass the key/value blocks around a ring, so each GPU sees every part without holding it all.

how.title: Look at fewer words
how.html: Sliding-window, sparse and linear attention cut the work itself by letting each word look at only some others, at some cost in accuracy.

demo.html: Match each memory or speed problem to the technique that fixes it.

example.html:
The online softmax. Scores [2, 1, 3, 0] in two blocks. After block 1 the running sum is e⁰ + e⁻¹ = 1.368 with max 2. Block 2 brings a bigger max (3), so the old sum is shrunk by e⁻¹: 0.503, plus e⁰ + e⁻³ gives 1.553, exactly what the full softmax would compute.

Supplementary bf16 has the same range as 32-bit numbers but fewer digits, so it rarely needs loss scaling; that is why most recent training uses it.

misunderstandings: Mixed precision halves all training memory.
Mainly activations; the fp32 master copy and Adam stay.
It is exact; only the order of work changes.
Ring Attention removes the n² cost.
It spreads the work across devices.
Adam's states are the biggest single part.
takeaways: Memory: weights, gradients, optimizer states, activations.
Mixed precision: 16-bit maths, fp32 master weights, loss scaling.
Attention is O(n²); FlashAttention tiles it exactly with an online softmax.
Ring Attention spreads long sequences; sparse/linear variants trade accuracy for scale.
thirty: Training is memory-bound. GPU memory holds weights, gradients, optimizer states and activations; activations (≈ 34·s·b·h·L bytes in 16-bit) grow with batch and sequence length and can exceed the weights' bill; checkpointing recomputes them. Adam in fp32 costs 4 + 4 + 8 = 16 bytes per parameter (1B → 16 GB before activations); sharding (ZeRO/FSDP) splits it across GPUs. Mixed precision does maths and stores activations in fp16/bf16, keeps an fp32 master copy, and uses loss scaling so small fp16 gradients (10⁻⁸) don't underflow; bf16 has fp32's range. Attention's score matrix is n × n: doubling n quadruples cost, and at 128k tokens one head's matrix would be ~33 GB. FlashAttention tiles Q, K, V in on-chip SRAM with an online softmax, giving exact results with far less memory traffic. Ring Attention passes K/V blocks around devices so context scales with device count. Sparse, sliding-window and linear attention reduce the work itself at some cost in quality.
